p.seg: The "New Discourses of Huánzǐ"
Qín's Lǚ Bùwéi invited the most sublime talents,
and produced the "Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǚ";
Hàn's Huáinán King employed the world's eloquent masters,
to compose literary works.
When the books were completed,
they were displayed in the capital markets,
with a thousand pieces of gold suspended,
to invite and show all scholars,
yet none could alter them.
This is because their content was concise and elegant,
complete in form yet subtle in expression.
See the commentary in "Wénxuǎn·Yáng Dézǔ".
Dǒng Zhòngshū dedicated himself to elucidating antiquity,
and even after reaching over sixty years of age,
he never glanced at the vegetables in his garden.
See "Imperial Readings" 976.
I composed the "New Discourses",
discoursing on past and present methods,
also wishing to promote governance.
How does it differ from the praise and blame of the "Spring and Autumn Annals"?
Now there are doubters,
so-called "clams differing from mussels",
"two and five not making ten."
Tán saw Liú Xiàng's "New Prefaces",
and Lù Jiǎ's "New Sayings",
then composed the "New Discourses".
Zhuāng Zhōu's fables,
even said:
"Yáo consulted Confucius."
"Huáinánzǐ" says:
"Gònggōng contended for emperorship,
causing the earth's cords to snap."
These are also fabrications.
Therefore, many in the world say:
"Short writings are unusable."
Yet in discussing the heavens,
none are clearer than the sages;
Zhuāng Zhōu and others, though fanciful,
should still have their good points selected,
why say to discard them entirely?
See "Imperial Readings" 602.
Now, the emperors,
followed by the three sovereigns and five hegemons,
these are the foremost rulers of the world.
Thus it is said the three august sovereigns governed by the Way,
while the five emperors transformed through virtue;
the three kings followed benevolence and righteousness,
the five hegemons employed power and wisdom.
The explanation goes:
Having no decrees
or punishments,
is called august sovereign;
having decrees
but no punishments,
is called emperor;
rewarding good and punishing evil,
with feudal lords paying court,
is called king;
raising armies,
swearing alliances,
correcting the world with trust and righteousness,
is called hegemon.
A king is one to whom people go,
meaning his beneficence is ample,
and the world turns to him.
Before the five emperors is too remote,
with no events in classics or commentaries.
Only the principles of the two peaks of king and hegemon,
determine the rationale of past and present.
The governance of the kingly way,
first eliminates human harms,
and provides ample food and clothing;
then teaches rites and propriety,
so they know likes, dislikes, approaches, and avoidances.
Thus, great transformation converges from all sides,
and the world is peaceful and joyful.
This is the method of kings.
The great achievements of hegemons,
honor the ruler and humble the ministers,
authority is unified,
government has no dual sources,
rewards and punishments are trustworthy,
laws and decrees are clear,
officials are well-ordered,
and authority is necessarily implemented.
This is the method of hegemons.
Kingly way is pure,
its virtue is like that;
hegemonic way is mixed,
its achievements are like this.
Both possess the world,
rule the myriad people,
bequeath lineage to descendants,
their essence is one.
See "Forest of Ideas", "Records of the Grand Historian·Qín Basic Annals" commentary, "The Extended Classic·Comprehensive Changes", "Imperial Readings" 77, and also 403.
Tāng and Wǔ long held positions as feudal lords and regional chiefs,
their virtue and kindness extended to the common people.
See commentary in "Wénxuǎn·Canonical Citations".
The ruler of the kingly way,
his virtue can bear,
encompassing to unify the primal heaven.
See "Initial Records" 9.
Some Confucians say:
"If aiming for kingship fails,
the alternative can be hegemony."
This statement is incorrect!
The tradition says:
"Among Confucius' disciples,
even a child of five feet,
does not speak of the five hegemons' affairs,
detesting their violation of benevolence and righteousness
and exaltation of power and deceit."
See "Forest of Ideas", "Imperial Readings" 77.
In governing a state,
the foundation of assistance,
lies in employing all with great talent.
Great talent is the ruler's limbs and wings.
See "Forest of Ideas".
Kings and dukes rejoice in obtaining good teachers and wise assistants,
common people delight in nurturing benevolent, worthy, and wise scholars,
all are the state's pillars and people's wings.
See "Imperial Readings" 187.
Kings are easy to assist,
hegemons are hard to support.
See "Forest of Ideas·Rènzǐ" quoting Huán Tán.
In the past, Yīnyǐn of Yīn,
Tàigōng of Zhōu,
Bǎilǐ Xī of Qín,
though all had great talent,
were all over seventy years old,
before becoming teachers to kings and hegemons.
See "Imperial Readings" 404.
In the past, the King of Qín saw the Zhōu court
lose order, ceding power to feudal lords,
and thought he should preserve the nine provinces.
Seeing the myriad people common,
like a flock of sheep or herd of pigs,
all drivable with a pole,
thus he became self-reliant,
not appointing others
or enfeoffing feudal lords.
Then Chén Shèng, Chǔ, and Hàn,
all rose from commoners,
not enfiefed lords with land,
yet together destroyed Qín,
leading to its defeat.
Emperor Gāo, having stabilized the realm,
reflected that King Xiàng entered from Hángǔ Pass,
while he himself arrived from Wǔguān Pass,
strengthened passes
and reinforced defenses,
internally充实ing the three armies,
externally increasing garrison posts,
established laws to thoroughly investigate cliques,
and heavily rewarded reports of rebellion.
When Wáng Wēng seized power,
he did not assault passes or strongholds,
but effortlessly obtained the position,
Wáng Wēng, seeing he gained it by controlling the state and governance,
suppressed powerful ministers,
centralized lower-level authority,
ensuring all matters, big or small, deep or shallow,
were decided by himself.
When he lost it,
it did not stem from the ministers.
Emperor Gèngshǐ, seeing Wáng Wēng lost the people's hearts
and the world,
upon reaching the western capital,
relied on the people's joy,
indulged in ease and pleasure,
ignored advice from remonstrating ministers and strategists,
while Chìméi besieged from outside,
and close ministers rebelled within the city,
leading to defeat.
From this perspective,
calamities and anomalies vary,
how can one set complete defenses and preparations?
The best preparation
is only to measure wise and greatly talented individuals,
then foresee and plan in advance,
to prevent and rescue accordingly.
See "Essentials of Governance from Various Books".
Bright mirrors are like turtle shells for divination.
Regulations are like measuring vessels.
Weighing scales are like rulers and measuring cords.
See Yì Lín.
Only acupuncture and herbal prescriptions
are tools for curing diseases,
which none but skilled physicians can use to heal people.
Talent, ability, virtue, and conduct
are instruments for governing a state,
which none but enlightened rulers can use to achieve merits.
If a physician lacks needles and medicines,
they can seek to purchase them
to practice their healing arts—
there is no need to necessarily possess them personally;
if a ruler lacks talent and virtue,
they can select and appoint enlightened assistants—
there is no need to personally possess all abilities.
From this we observe
that talent, ability, virtue, and conduct
are the state's acupuncture and medicine.
The achievement of merits and effects
lies in the ruler's assistants.
The tradition says:
"Obtaining ten fine horses
is not as good as obtaining one Bó Lè;
obtaining ten sharp swords
is not as good as obtaining one Ōu Yě."
Acquiring many fine things
is not as good as acquiring a few who can recognize things.
Those who recognize things can bring forth excellent treasures,
and treasures will increasingly abound—
not limited to merely ten.
See Qún Shū Zhì Yào.
Summon the talents of the nine provinces to court.
See Běi Táng Shū Chāo, chapter 11.
In ancient times, Yáo tested Shùn at the Great Slope. The "slope"
meant overseeing and recording the affairs of the world,
similar to the office of Shàngshū today.
One should obtain great sages and wise men
to enable them to deliberate and maintain fairness.
See annotations to Xù Hàn‧Bǎi Guān Zhì, Běi Táng Shū Chāo chapter 59, Yì Wén Lèi Jù chapter 48, Tài Píng Yù Lǎn chapter 212.
In the past, Zhōu Gōng glorified the way of the Zhōu,
and his beneficence reached to the four corners.
See annotations to Wén Xuǎn‧Shí Quē Míng.
Administering justice as impartially as water.
See Běi Táng Shū Chāo chapter 44.
Sages appear only once in a thousand years,
and even worthies and noble men, though they long and ponder,
cannot easily see one.

See annotations to Wén Xuǎn‧Liú Yuèshí's "Exhortation to Advance," annotations to "Eulogy on Three Kingdoms Ministers," annotations to "Discourse on Board Games," annotations to "Lament for Wèi Wǔ Dì."
For straightforwardness and loyal integrity, there was Jí Àn's courage in admonishing and disputing.
See annotations to Wén Xuǎn‧"Policy Questions for Xiùcai in the Third Year of Tiānjiān."
Outstanding men of former generations,
who achieved merits and left a lasting name,
had their portraits displayed in palaces, halls, and government offices—
these are the state's great treasures,
truly priceless!
Even amassing Hé's jade,
accumulating Xià's jade pendants,
filling bags with Suí Hóu's pearls,
and boxing luminous night-shining pearls
would not suffice as a metaphor.
Figures like Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Shàng, Zhāng Liáng, and Chén Píng—
in which era are they absent?
But if the ruler does not recognize them,
the ministers remain unused.
See Yì Lín.
To capture fierce beasts,
one does not have a beauty raise her hand;
to catch huge fish,
one does not let a child lightly participate.
It is not for lack of closeness,
but because their strength is inadequate.
How then can the lord of ten thousand chariots
not select the right people?
See Cháng Duǎn Jīng‧Shì Fēi quoting Huán Zǐ.
Biographical records say:
Wèi Móu went north to see the King of Zhào,
who was having a hatter make a cap in front of him,
and asked Móu about governing the state.
Móu replied:
"If Your Majesty could value the state as much as this two-foot ribbon,
then the state would be well-governed and secure."
The king said:
"The state inherited from my ancestors,
with its ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain, is of utmost importance—
how can you compare it to a two-foot ribbon?"
Móu said:
"When Your Majesty has a cap made,
you do not use close attendants
but necessarily seek a craftsman—
is it not because a ruined ribbon would mean the cap is unfinished?
Now if the state is poorly governed,
the altars of soil and grain will be unstable,
and the ancestral temples will receive no sacrifices.
If Your Majesty does not seek excellent scholars
but appoints those you privately favor,
is this not valuing the state less than the making of a two-foot ribbon?"
The king had no reply.
See Běi Táng Shū Chāo chapter 127, Tài Píng Yù Lǎn chapter 824.
Human nature is generally hard to fathom
and difficult to know.
Thus, those who are exceptionally different
are often overlooked by the common world.
See annotations to Wén Xuǎn‧"Returning Home," annotations to the preface of "Collection of Wáng Wénxiàn."
There was an old man named Xuē,
an expert horse physiognomist of Cháng'ān.
He obtained a fine horse from a border commandery,
ugly in appearance but correct in gait,
named Colt.
When ridden into the market,
people did not notice its coming and going.
Later, when questioned earnestly,
they requested to see it.
The old man said:
"You gentlemen have no eye for horses,
so it's not worth showing you."
See Yì Wén Lèi Jù chapter 93, annotations to Wén Xuǎn‧"Rhapsody on Shǔ Capital," Tài Píng Yù Lǎn chapter 897.
Though livestock are lowly,
there are exceptionally good ones among them,
all recorded and remembered.
Thus, horses are praised as Huá, Liú, Jì,
and Lù; oxen are famed as Guō Jiāo and Dīng Lì.
See Yì Wén Lèi Jù chapter 94.
Worthies have five grades:
Those careful and diligent in household affairs,
obedient and fraternal among kin and neighbors,
are the scholars of the village;
those robust and intelligent,
flawless in letters and law,
are the scholars of the county court;
those sincere, trustworthy, steadfast in conduct,
upright, fair,
managing subordinates and serving superiors with principle,
are the scholars of the commandery;
those versed in classics and arts,
of high reputation and conduct,
capable in administration,
broad-minded, harmonious, and firm in integrity,
are the scholars for high ministers and assistants;
those of supreme and unparalleled talent,
distinctly different from the masses,
with great strategies and many plans,
able to plan for the age and achieve merits,
are the scholars for the empire.
See Yì Lín.
Living at home following principles,
harmonious and compliant in the neighborhood,
respectful in coming and going,
cautious and humble in speech—
these are called good scholars.
See annotations to Wén Xuǎn‧Fàn Yèzōng's "Discourse on Eunuchs."
Speaking of the methods to seek assistants,
once obtained,
there are three major difficulties
and two impediments to goodness.
In worldly affairs,
the mediocre are many,
and great talents few;
the few cannot overcome the many,
one mouth cannot dispute a whole state.
Holding a solitary, unique view,
opposing popular consensus,
from a remote and humble position,
resisting the minds of the noble and base,
then nothing will align.
This is the first difficulty!
To establish extraordinary deeds,
to do the unusual,
is what the common world cannot perceive.
Moreover, having the wise plan affairs
and then leveling them with the multitude
will surely be insufficient.
This is the second difficulty!
Even if heard and accepted,
and some measures are implemented,
before the task is completed,
slanderers follow and vilify it,
causing doubt midway,
or making the speaker suffer blame instead.
This is the third difficulty!
The wise exhaust their hearts and offer advice,
striving to achieve things for the state;
when the multitude hears of it,
they are instead suspected,
and if one thing does not fit,
they are slandered and maligned—
even with ten good deeds,
one fault can obscure and remove them.
This is the first impediment to goodness!
Talented individuals are often envied by the world.
Only when encountering an enlightened ruler
do they rise together.
Even if fortunate to gain such opportunity,
they may still follow the crowd,
unable to share understanding with the wise.
Even someone like Zhòngní
would depart if unrecognized.
This exemplifies the virtue of knowing when to stop!
Thus, unless ruler and minister establish intimate, firm trust,
opening their hearts to believe in each other,
acting without suspicion—
like Yī and Lǚ being employed,
Fù Yuè encountered in dreams,
or Guǎn and Bào's mutual faith—
it is difficult to achieve accomplishments and fulfill intentions.
Moreover, persuasive speech takes many forms:
those wishing to impress envoys
cite ancient worthy assistants who admonished rulers,
while those seeking to sow discord
discuss those who endangered states by monopolizing power.
Even between father and son—the closest relationship—
rulers have instances like Gāozōng and Xiàojǐ.
During the reigns of Jǐng and Wǔ,
affairs of Lì and Crown Prince Wèi occurred,
while loyal ministers of high integrity
sometimes faced tragedies like Lóng Péng, Bǐ Gān,
Wǔ Yún, and Cháo Cuò.
Such examples are too numerous
to record completely.
How then can one act?
How easily can one understand?
Nevertheless,
examining the proven effects of past generations
provides both insight
and warning.
All profoundly talented individuals
facing timely misfortunes
aspire to match the worthies above,
leaving glory through the ages.
Why would they ruin their reputation, abandon righteousness,
and commit treacherous deeds?
Consider Lǔ Lián declining gold and fiefs from Qí and Zhào,
or Yú Qīng sacrificing a marquisate and chancellorship—
they delighted in achieving fame and fulfilling aspirations,
would they again seek flattery and profit?
Observing all treacherous, rebellious ministers,
they are merely clever-tongued, greedy individuals!
None are among the greatly talented.
From this perspective,
the world's extraordinary scholars of supreme talent
clearly demonstrate trustworthy conduct,
yet mediocre rulers suspect them.
If unable to listen and adopt
their strategies,
even with broad knowledge and attainment,
it ultimately proves futile.
From "Essentials of Governance from Various Books".
Had Jiǎ Yì not been demoted and frustrated,
his literary brilliance would not have emerged;
had Huáinán not been noble and wealthy,
he could not have broadly recruited talents
to compose writings and books;
had Grand Historian Sīmǎ not overseen records,
he could not systematically detail past and present;
had Yáng Xióng not been poor,
he could not have written "Mystical" and "Sayings".
From "Forest of Ideas".
The three benevolent men of Yīn
were obscure beforehand
but illustrious afterward.
What benefit to affairs?
What aid to the ruler?
From "Forest of Ideas".
Speaking to Yáng Zǐyún:
"If later ages produce another sage,
people will only recognize his talents surpass theirs,
mostly unable to discern whether he is sage or not."
Zǐyún said:
"Indeed so."
From "Lùn Héng · Discussing Auspicious Signs".
What ordinary people hear and see,
know and recognize in their minds,
love and hate by nature,
avoid and pursue for profit or harm—
all share common endeavors.
If talents differ in magnitude,
wisdom in depth,
acuity in perception,
and substance in character—
all vary in degree.
Without great talent and deep wisdom,
one cannot perceive the greater scheme.
The greater scheme
means acting appropriately in all matters.
Speaking rightly and planning fittingly,
employing flexibility amid change,
constantly maintaining integrity,
remaining unconfused when events arise,
having inner measure
that cannot be swayed or deceived by cunning strangeness—
this constitutes understanding the greater scheme!
Without great talent,
even with authority like Wáng Wēng,
discernment like Gōngsūn Lóng,
wit like Dōngfāng Shuò,
interpreting portents like Jīng Jūnming,
or broad knowledge and extensive learning,
reading up to ten thousand volumes,
teaching hundreds or thousands as a Confucian scholar—
only increases ignorance of the greater scheme!
Wáng Wēng's faults surpassing ordinary people were three:
his wisdom sufficient to conceal wrong and seize right,
debate able to exhaustively interrogate persuaders,
authority to intimidate all subordinates.
Moreover, he frequently secretly struck against those displeasing him,
so no minister could oppose his arguments,
none dared confront or admonish him,
ultimately leading to ruin and defeat.
Such is the disaster of ignoring the greater scheme!
The greater scheme for emperors
is exemplified by Emperor Gāo.
Emperor Gāo said:
"Zhāng Liáng, Xiāo Hé, Hán Xìn—
these three men
are all outstanding figures.
I could employ them,
thus gaining the empire."
This shows the effect of understanding the greater scheme!
When Wáng Wēng first held state power,
he considered himself comprehensively wise and sagely,
believing no subordinate's ability surpassed his.
Thus in initiating actions and affairs,
he always desired self-reliance,
unwilling to consult various knowledgeable experts.
Deploying troops merely on whim,
using whatever he obtained,
he rarely achieved effective results,
thus suddenly meeting defeat and destruction.
This is ignorance of the greater scheme!
Emperor Gāo, possessing great wisdom and strategy,
could self-measure,
and when ministers established affairs and laws,
often said:
"Set them low, not high,
according to what I can implement."
Regulations were internally relaxed,
governance suited the times,
thus people and ministers delighted,
remembered by later generations.
This is understanding the greater scheme!
Wáng Wēng admired ancient sage governance,
but disparaged Hàn dynasty laws,
thus frequently making changes,
attempting every matter to imitate antiquity,
praising former sage institutions,
yet unaware he could not implement them,
abandoning the near for the distant,
advocating impracticalities,
thus through lofty ideals
led to decline and chaos.
This is ignorance of the greater scheme!
Emperor Gāo, wishing to attack Wèi,
sent spies to observe its chancellor
and various generals, officers, and key aides,
learning their names,
then said:
"These all fall short of my Xiāo Hé,
Cáo Cān, Hán Xìn, Fán Kuài, etc.,
they're easily handled!"
Thereupon he attacked
and defeated them.
This is understanding the greater scheme!
Wáng Wēng earlier desired to campaign north against Xiōngnú,
later east against Qīng, Xú provinces' Red Eyebrows rebels,
yet never selected skilled generals,
but only used hereditary families or cautious clerks,
sometimes dispending close relatives, sons, grandsons
personally favored,
or those lacking command wisdom for generalship.
To recklessly appoint someone to command troops and control the masses,
facing formidable enemies,
thus when the army assembles it suffers losses,
and the soldiers scatter and flee.
The fault lies in not selecting the right general,
for both the general and the sovereign lack understanding of the greater scheme of things!
See Qún Shū Zhì Yào.
Move like a thunderclap,
stand firm like a mountain,
attack like a lightning strike,
capture like a swift wind,
light in the front and heavy in the rear,
solid within and void without.
See Běi Táng Shū Chāo, chapter 116.
The strict, fierce, and roaring methods of Zhōu Yàfū
can be said to exemplify a great general of the state.
See the unrevised edition of Běi Táng Shū Chāo, chapter 115.
There exists in the world the game of wéiqí,
some say it is akin to military strategy.
When playing it,
the superior player places stones distantly and spreads them out, positioning them
to encircle,
thereby attacking,
achieving victory by mastering the principles.
The average player
focuses on cutting off and blocking key points,
striving for advantage and profit,
thus the outcome remains uncertain,
requiring calculation to decide.
The inferior player
guards the corners,
hastily creating small territories,
seeking to survive in confined spaces,
yet still inevitably falls short.
Consider the words of Xuē Gōng regarding Qíng Bù's rebellion:
The superior strategy stated: seize Wú and Chǔ,
annex Qí, Lǔ, Yān, and Zhào—
this refers to expanding territorial influence.
The middle strategy stated: seize Wú and Chǔ,
annex Hán and Wèi,
block the Chénggāo Pass,
occupy the Áo Granary—
this is striving for key advantages and contending for profit.
The inferior strategy stated: seize Wú and Xiàcài,
occupy Chángshā
to press against Yuè—
this is guarding the corners,
hastily creating small territories.
The generals and ministers of Gēngshǐ Emperor failed in defense,
allowing the central "dead stones" in wéiqí to come to life.
See Collected Commentaries on Shǐ Jì: Biography of Qíng Bù, annotation in Wén Xuǎn: Essay on Board Games, Cháng Duǎn Jīng chapter 2: State Power, Tài Píng Yù Lǎn chapter 753, and Yì Lín.
When Gēngshǐ Emperor arrived in Cháng'ān,
his high officials assigned themselves to affairs of the Eastern Palace,
earning ridicule from their subordinates.
They merely built small guard towers,
occupying half the city to reside—
from this, it is clear their generals and ministers were no match for Xiāo Hé or Cáo Shěn.
See Chū Xué Jì, chapter 24.
In speech and action, what matters is excellence and virtue,
not abundance.
Utter one excellent word or perform one virtuous deed,
and all under heaven will follow.
If one evil intention or disgraceful act is seen,
the myriad people will turn away.
Can one not be cautious?
Thus the Yì Jīng says:
"Speech and action are the pivotal mechanism of the noble person;
the movement of this pivot
determines honor or disgrace,
and is what moves heaven and earth."
See Qún Shū Zhì Yào.
Wáng Wēng executed people with punishments,
and further inflicted cruel harm.
He went so far as to burn people alive,
pouring the "five poisons" into the muscles of the deceased.
When burying them,
he again covered them with thorns.
Once a person is dead,
they are no different from earth or wood—
what gain or loss is there in inflicting further cruelty?
Chéng Tāng's reflection and acceptance
brought no material benefit to the people,
yet the people turned to him
because they praised his virtuous kindness;
King Xuān of Qí sparing an ox
provided no advantage to the worthy,
yet the worthy approved of him
because they valued his humane heart;
King Wén burying exposed bones
offered no practical help to the masses,
yet the masses were pleased
because his kindness and righteousness moved them.
Wáng Wēng's mutilation of the dead,
inspecting their five organs,
caused no harm to the living,
yet the living detested him
because he displayed extreme cruelty.
These four cases,
though subtle, are profoundly revealing;
though minute, their significance is great.
Thus two sages rose to prominence,
one ruler was praised,
while Wáng Wēng perished—
showing how vast is the difference between understanding the greater scheme and failing to do so!
See Qún Shū Zhì Yào.
When a sage king governs the state,
he exalts ritual and deference,
manifests humaneness and righteousness,
and focuses on honoring the worthy and loving the people.
Thus, divination is seldom used,
and sacrifices are sparse.
See Qún Shū Zhì Yào.
Formerly, King Líng of Chǔ was arrogant, dissolute, and contemptuous of subordinates,
neglected the worthy and devoted himself to ghosts,
believed in the ways of shamans and invokers,
fasted and purified himself,
to sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
and performed rituals for his ministers.
Personally holding feather ornaments,
he danced before the altar.
When the men of Wú came to attack,
and his people reported the emergency,
King Líng continued dancing and drumming unperturbed,
turning to respond:
"I am currently sacrificing to the Supreme Deity,
delighting the bright spirits—
I should receive blessed protection,
and dare not go to rescue."
Thereupon the Wú troops arrived,
capturing his crown prince and consorts—
truly lamentable.

Wáng Wēng favored divination,
believed in auspicious days,
and was fervent in serving ghosts and spirits.
He built many temple grounds,
purifying himself and conducting sacrifices.
The expense of sacrificial animals and offerings,
and the toil of officials and soldiers in preparations,
were beyond description!
His governance was poor,
and he was betrayed by all under heaven.
When disaster struck and armies rose,
he had no strategy to save or extricate himself.
He then raced to the southern suburb to pray,
clutching his chest to proclaim his grievance,
crying out with flowing tears,
kowtowing to beg for his life,
hoping for heaven's pity and aid.
When troops entered his palace that day,
arrows flew thick as rain,
fires blazed fiercely—
fleeing beneath the Jiàn Terrace,
he still clung to his mandate texts and crafted power-measuring vessel—
truly the height of delusion!

Dōngfāng Shuò's brief and plain words
were considered trustworthy and verified.
People all said Shuò possessed great wisdom,
unmatched by later worthies.

or a sè for a kōnghóu—
this is not only not knowing the fox and the sè,
but also not knowing the raccoon dog and the kōnghóu.
Thus, it is not only misjudging Shuò,
but also not knowing later worthies."

I previously served as Director of Music,
when an owl hooted in a tree in the courtyard,
causing worry and fear among the officials.
Later, I fought with Marquis Xiè, the Director of Music,
and both were dismissed from our posts.

and fell ill on the journey.
Wrapped in a wadded quilt,
wearing a crimson
woolen cloak, and riding a red horse,
I lodged at the eastern lodge of Xiàyì.
The station master suspected I was a bandit,
and sent soldiers to attack by night.
I ordered my attendants not to fight,
and after questioning, they departed.
This is how stillness preserves oneself.

If someone speaks well of me to others,
they will surely speak ill of me to others as well.
Wáng Wēng sent Commandant Mèng Sūn to Tài Shān to offer sacrifices,
passing through Xúzhōu on the way.
The Governor of Xúzhōu, Sòng Zhòngwēng,
praised my talent and wisdom,
comparing me to Chén Píng and Liú Hóu.
When Mèng Sūn returned,
he joyfully said to me:
"Zhòngwēng praised your great virtue,
is this truly what you are like?"
I replied:
"Having traveled with me for four or five years,
you never praised me.
Now hearing Zhòngwēng's single remark
you find it strange;
if someone were to slander me,
you would believe it too—
I fear you!"
See "Yilin".

"Retiring plumply, nothing is unfavorable."
See commentary to Xiè Língyùn's "Entering Huázigǎng Poem" in "Wenxuan".
King Kāng of Sòng wore a headless crown,
to display his courage.
See "Taiping Yulan" juan 684.
Historical records say:
Chúnyú Kūn visited a neighbor's house,
saw their straight chimney flue,
with firewood piled beside it,
and said:
"This will cause a fire disaster."
He advised them to make the flue curved,
and move the firewood far away.
The household didn't listen,
later disaster struck,
fire indeed reached the piled wood
and burned their house.
Neighbors together helped fight the fire,
before extinguishing it.
Then they cooked mutton and prepared wine,
to reward those who helped put out the fire.
But they definitely wouldn't invite Chúnyú Kūn to drink and eat
for advising the curved flue and distant firewood.
A wise man ridiculed this, saying:
"Those who teach others to curve flues and move firewood
receive no gratitude,
while those with scorched heads and burned foreheads
become honored guests instead."
This laments how they value the trivial
while neglecting the fundamental.
Is this only true for chimney flues and firewood in preventing harm?
Human ailments and state chaos,
are all like this too.
Thus good doctors treat illness before it manifests,
and wise rulers cut off plots at their root.
Later generations often fail at preventing problems before they sprout,
while diligently attacking them after they've formed,
strategic ministers rarely receive rewards,
while combat soldiers often gain glory.
Like those people,
they nearly miss what's important in affairs,
examining Chúnyú Kūn's prediction,
one can understand everything.
This is the category of perceiving subtle signs.
See "Qunshu Zhiyao".
Academician disciple Hán Shēng lived at the eastern temple,
had ominous dreams for three consecutive nights,
and asked others about it.
Someone advised him to get up at dawn
and pray with a purified heart.
After three mornings,
someone accused him of cursing others,
he was arrested and tried,
and died after several days.
See "Taiping Yulan" juan 186 and also juan 400.
Attendant Jǐng Zǐchūn was skilled in divination,
but was imprisoned due to some matter.
His father-in-law Ruò Zhū came to the prison gate,
sending word that he left trousers and a jacket.
Zǐchūn exclaimed in surprise:[88"Did Master Zhū come to speak?
'Zhū' means 'execute',
trousers with a jacket,
means being cut off at the middle.
I will be executed and severed."
Later he was indeed cut in half at the waist.
See "Taiping Yulan" juan 695.
Yángchéngzǐ's surname was Zhāng, given name Héng,
from Shǔ Commandery.
Wáng Wēng and I both served as Lecturers and Sacrificial Wine,
when he fell critically ill,
he pre-purchased a coffin,
placing many brocades inside,
which immediately led to his grave being robbed after burial.
See "Taiping Yulan" juan 815.
All first established the fundamental,
widely set up protective screens,
to build their own factions,
and strengthen the state's foundation.
Thus when King Wǔ of Zhōu conquered Yīn,
before even descending his carriage he enfeoffed the descendants of Huángdì,
Yáo, Shùn, Xià, and Yīn,
along with relatives of the same surname,
meritorious officials, and virtuous men,
as his wings.
Assisting the great enterprise,
eternally passing it down to later generations.
Then the powerful Qín abolished the feudal lords,
relying solely on themselves,
entrusting everything to one person,
not enfeoffing any sons or brothers,
leaving them isolated and weak with no support,
thus their empire lasted only fourteen years before falling.
When Hàn Gāozǔ first stabilized the realm,
he rejected the failed policies of fallen Qín,
following the wise ways of Yīn and Zhōu,
honoring and highlighting merit and virtue,
generously enfeoffing sons and brothers.
Although many later failed due to arrogance and excess,
still Hàn's foundation
was thereby secured,
and powerful ministers of different surnames
could no longer overthrow it.
By the time of Emperor Jǐng and Emperor Wǔ,
seeing the various kings frequently rebel,
they suppressed and seized their power,
leaving the kings only empty titles,
living off land taxes.
Thus the Hàn court weakened,
standing isolated and alone,
so Wáng Wēng raised no troops to command officers,
but directly seized the empire.
Moreover, harboring greedy desires for exclusive achievement and profit,
he refused to enfeoff sons, grandsons, or relatives of the same surname,
as protective bulwarks for stability,
so when troops rose, he had no one to rescue him.
The tradition says:
"Those who share the same ailment as a dead person
cannot act as doctors;
those who implement the same governance as a fallen state
cannot be consulted for plans."
Wáng Wēng's actions closely resembled tyrannical Qín,
thus he also lost his empire after fifteen years.
Those who hunt and shoot birds and beasts,
initially want to hit them,
fearing the wound won't be large enough;
but after catching them,
they dislike that too much meat is damaged.
A vulgar man obtained some meat sauce and found it delicious,
at mealtime,
he disliked sharing it with others,
so he spat a little into it.
Those who would share it grew angry,
then threw the sauce on the ground,
so it was discarded
and none could eat it!
Those fallen Qín and Wáng Wēng,
when wanting to seize the empire,
were happy to share it with others;
but after obtaining it, treasured it too much to share—
this is like the meat-spitting sauce case.
See "Qunshu Zhiyao".
Once Duke Huán of Qí went out,
saw some old ruins
and asked about them.
Someone replied:
"These are the ruins of the Guō family."
He asked again:
"Why did the Guō family become ruins?"
The reply:
"They praised the good and hated the evil."
Duke Huán said:
"Praising good and hating evil should make them survive,
yet instead they became ruins—
why?"
The answer:
"They praised the good but couldn't employ them,
hated the evil but couldn't remove them.
The good people, knowing they were valued but not employed,
resented them;
the evil people, seeing they were despised and disliked,
hated them."
To harbor grudges against good people,
and bear enmity towards evil ones,
can one avoid ruin?"
Previously, Wáng Wēng was fond of the worthy, wise, and talented scholars of the world,
gathering them through summons
but unwilling to employ them.
This caused people to hold slander and resent him;
Emperor Gēngshǐ detested the various kings and those who falsely claimed titles without righteousness,
yet could not remove them,
making each harbor hatred and enmity towards him.
Thus, Wáng Wēng was attacked and died,
his palaces burned to the ground;
Emperor Gēngshǐ was forced to flee by the various kings with false titles,
leaving the city walls in ruins.
Both rulers incurred the cost of favoring the good and disfavoring the evil,
so they could not escape calamitous disasters,
ultimately causing the great capital Cháng'ān
to be destroyed and reduced to ruins,
an act of great wrongdoing.
The ancestors of the northern barbarians,
coexisted with the Central Kingdom,
for many years,
too numerous to record.
The benevolent could not win them over with virtue;
the strong could not subdue them by force!
Their nature is fierce and violent,
gathering like beasts and scattering like birds;
their strength is hard to subdue,
and their submission difficult to obtain.
Thus, sage kings controlled them loosely
without imposing strict rule.
In the past, when the Zhōu dynasty declined,
the Yí and Dí tribes repeatedly invaded,
leaving the Central Kingdom hanging by a thread.
Then King Xuān restored the dynasty,
barely recovering the invaded territories.
Even with Qín Shǐhuáng's might,
leading four hundred thousand armored troops,
he could not penetrate west of the Yellow River,
so he built the Great Wall to separate them.
When the Hàn rose,
Emperor Gāozǔ was besieged at Píngchéng;
during Empress Lǚ's time, there were treacherous words;
under Emperor Wén, the Xiōngnú invaded deeply,
with beacon fires and scout cavalry
reaching Yōng Gānquán;
between Emperors Jǐng and Wǔ,
military campaigns were repeatedly thwarted,
ultimately failing to capture or control them,
so they made peace through marriage alliances.
Only then did the borders gain peace,
and the Central Kingdom became tranquil.
Later, the Xiōngnú had internal strife,
dividing into five Chányús.
Gān Yánshòu capitalized on their weakness,
showing deep kindness to Hūhánxié Chányú,
who thus willingly submitted and pledged allegiance,
coming to pay homage to the Hàn court.
The Hàn court could proclaim its virtue and expand its glory,
displaying majesty to the four seas,
with all submitting,
and no invasions for generations.
Before stability or danger could be determined,
they rashly oppressed the Xiōngnú again,
attacking to seize their seals and ribbons,
demoting their ministers' titles and ranks,
changing old customs,
and dividing the Chányú into fifteen.
This caused great resentment and fury,
leading to mutual attacks and resistance.
Wáng Wēng did not blame or regret himself,
but instead persisted in unyielding and unreasonable actions,
appointing many generals,
mobilizing troops and horses,
transporting and relocating grain and supplies,
to exhaust the resources of the world.
The world was filled with sorrow, hatred, and suffering,
leading to great turmoil,
yet they could not defeat a single Hú barbarian,
only exhausting themselves to the extreme.
The Book of Documents says:
"Heaven's calamities can be avoided,
but those of one's own making cannot be escaped."
This is what it means!
When Emperor Gāozǔ was besieged,
he went ten days without food,
but upon escaping,
showed no anger.
Truly, he knew that past attacks were futile,
and resentment was useless.
Now the Xiōngnú betrayed Wáng Wēng,
and Wáng Wēng went to invade and harass them,
thus causing affairs to reach this state.
Is this not what is called
"meat breeds its own worms,
and humans bring their own disasters"!
It was unnecessary,
yet so severe,
truly the height of self-infliction.
From "Essentials of Governance from Various Books".

the people's annual tax revenue was over forty million strings of cash,

Abnormal and strange occurrences
are common in the world,
occurring in every era.
When met by enlightened rulers, worthy ministers, wise scholars, and benevolent people,
they cultivate virtue and good governance,
streamline duties and act cautiously in response.
Thus, calamities vanish,
and misfortune turns to blessing!
In the past, King Tài Wù faced the omen of mulberry and grain growing in the court,
and gained the title of Zhōngzōng;
Wǔ Dīng had the anomaly of a pheasant calling and alighting on a tripod,
and enjoyed a lifespan of a hundred years;
King Chéng of Zhōu encountered the portent of thunder and wind breaking trees,
and received the response of favorable winds and abundant harvests;
Duke Jǐng of Sòng worried about Mars stationed in the Heart constellation,
and the star moved three houses away.
From this, it is seen
that nothing is better than replying with virtue, righteousness, and sincerity!
Thus, the "Zhōu Shū" says:
"When the Son of Heaven sees an omen, he cultivates virtue;
when feudal lords see an omen, they improve governance;
when high officials see an omen, they fulfill their duties;
when scholars and commoners see an omen, they cultivate themselves.
Spirits cannot harm the Way,
and monsters cannot injure virtue."
In decadent ages with shallow customs,
rulers and ministers often become licentious, arrogant, and misgovern;
scholars and commoners often have wicked hearts and evil deeds.
Thus, disasters and anomalies frequently occur,
yet they do not introspect,
fear Heaven's majesty,
but instead seek external blame and criticism,
inquiring about the causes,
deceived by flatterers and fools
and thus misled,
allowing calamities to take hold,
all acting against Heaven and contrary to the Way!
From "Essentials of Governance from Various Books".

when dukes, ministers, and high officials gathered at court,
the chancellor said in conversation:
'I hear that when an owl gives birth,
the offspring grow up,
and will eat their mother,
only then can they fly—
is this true?'
Then a worthy man replied:
'I only hear that owlets feed their mother in return.'
The chancellor was greatly ashamed,
regretting his mistaken words.
All the scholars looked down on the chancellor
and praised that worthy man,
whose words
benefited moral transformation.

even birds and beasts are given the benefit of the doubt,
how much more so for people?

Some say:
"When high ministers and important officials were lacking in the past,
everyone would anticipate and arrange among themselves:

Later it indeed happened so.

and moreover were able to agree with the ruler's intention?"

not very far apart from each other.

are certainly known to both superiors and inferiors from before."
Those with clear differences see things differently,
those with equal wisdom consider things similarly,
therefore the hidden thoughts of the subordinates
often match the ruler's perspective.
Like when Tāng and Wǔ employed Yī and Lǚ,
Emperor Gāozōng employed Fù Yuè;
Huán and Mù appointed Guǎn, Nìng, Yóu, and Xī;

The state establishes judicial officers,
institutes criminal laws,
to suppress the wicked and evil;
moreover, internally appoints Zhōngchéng and Yùshǐ
to rectify the capital area,
therefore usually employing those well-versed in the law.
Initially intending to properly enforce the law,
but ending up either too lenient or too severe,
all strive for excessive cruelty.
Wishing to appear not to have spared effort,
and seeking to obtain merit rewards;
or wanting to establish achievements,
yet fearing slander of weakness,
therefore employing whips and clubs,
manipulating documents to create crimes,

Gradually reaching the court,

all becoming confused and critical.
Officials implementing severe measures,
say:
"If subordinates still enforce strictness,

Worthy officials and upright scholars
handling affairs for the ruler,
should uphold the law like clear colors!
Therefore, when speech is appropriate, it must be practicable;
when crime is appropriate, it must be punishable.
How can one arbitrarily seek to flatter and follow hints?
If encountering the ruler's neglect,
not staying overnight
but immediately implementing matters,
then one should expect violent death.

Since rulers are not understanding,
and assisting officials further follow along,
complying and completing it,

Drawing on water and carving ice,

presumptuously sought to equal him.

a small rhapsody about a certain matter,
applying such intense concentration
that I immediately became agitated and fell ill,
recovering only after many days.

During Emperor Chéng's time,
when Zhào Zhāoyí was greatly favored,
every time he went to Gānquán Palace,
he was ordered to compose a rhapsody,
doing so with sudden urgency,
his thoughts intensely focused.

he became so exhausted he lay down to rest,
dreaming that his five internal organs came out onto the ground,
and he gathered them with his hands and put them back inside.

he suffered from panting and palpitations,
with greatly reduced energy,
and was ill for a year.
From this we can say
that exhausting one's thoughts
injures the essential spirit.

then who goes first?

why cling to these moments?"

and saw in the musicians' records
this account:
"During Emperor Wén's time,
they found a musician named Dòu Gōng from Marquis Wén of Wèi's era,
who was 180 years old.

Emperor Wén, amazed, asked him:
'What regimen do you follow
that enables you to reach such an age?'

so they taught me music,
had me play the zither,
and daily practice became my constant activity.

I once visited my former colleague Dù Fáng,
who had been Magistrate of Chén,

achieving a lifespan of several hundred years.

can I truly prolong life and ward off aging?"
I answered him:
"Though we share the same form and name,
our inherent natures and capacities differ,
with variations in strength and fragility.
If you lovingly nurture and properly apply them,
you may merely fare slightly better.
This is like clothing, shoes, and utensils -
if you care for them, they remain intact,
and being complete, they last long."
I noticed a hemp candle beside him,
with a hanging wick-end about a foot long,
so I used it to illustrate my point,
saying:
"The essential spirit dwelling in the body
is like fire burning a candle.
If you properly tend it,
adjusting the candle as the flame requires,
it may not extinguish until the candle is finished.
Without the candle,
fire cannot travel alone through emptiness,
nor can it afterwards burn the
wick-end. The wick-end is like human old age -
teeth falling out, hair turning white,
muscles withering and drying up,
while the essential spirit cannot moisten
and permeate throughout the inside and outside.
Then the vital energy is exhausted and death comes,
just as both fire and candle are used up!
When people encounter pathogenic injury or illness,
but don't receive proper care or good physicians,
some die premature violent deaths.
In death, their muscles, sinews, and bones
are often as if fire were struck by a side wind
and cannot be rescued.
Also, when the Dào is extinguished,
then the skin remains while the stem lengthens.
I once sat drinking at night indoors,
lighting a hemp candle.
When the candle was half-burnt and about to go out,
I immediately examined it closely,
and seeing its peeling
and cracked skin, I adjusted and turned it,
whereupon the fire crossed over and revived.
Similarly, if the human body
suffers some damage or depletion,
but can be carefully nurtured and well maintained,
it may also recover.
"Moreover, since no one can remember their time of birth,
they should not expect to know about old age and death either.
In ancient times of peace and harmony,
people and things were born enveloped in beautiful abundance,
all robust and long-lived,
reaching around a hundred years before death.
Dying was then suddenly like lying down to sleep,
just as fruits and grains naturally fall when fully ripe.
Later generations encounter degenerate and malign influences,
marry at inappropriate times,
and labor excessively,
so both parents and children are injured,
with sinews, bones, blood, and energy not fully strong.
Hence many meet with misfortune and die early,
passing away in middle age.
When they encounter illness
or suffer painful distress,
then they are cut off prematurely.
Therefore they sigh, lament, and detest death,
considering it a great calamity.
Formerly, Duke Jǐng of Qí admired his state
and enjoyed its pleasures,
saying:
'If only in ancient times there had been no death,
how would it be?'"
Yàn Zǐ said:

while the malevolent perish in it.

daily studying to attain understanding,
so as to hasten to establish oneself and spread one's fame;
but instead merely covets profit and long life,

Someone objected, saying:

even with fire residing in it,
it cannot become whole again.
Thus, spirit and qi enable growth,
but unlike candle flame which cannot repair itself,
this is precisely where they differ.
Why then try to equate them?"
The response was:

should gradually emerge from within to merge with the outside.

but then regenerates.
This is similar to how human blood and qi nourish growth of muscles and flesh.
Considering their ultimate end,
some become embers,
some become dregs.
Why can this not serve as an analogy?"

I also recounted the previous burning hemp candle incident,

Exhaustion and replacement lie with others,

If their muscles, bones, blood and qi are full and strong,
then form and spirit branch and long life follows;
if defective then cut off and injured,
just as fire's speed depends on fat and wick's quantity and length.
Wanting lamps and candles to exhaust and replace themselves is impossible,

turn and rotate to steam dry, enabling fire to settle properly,

As for those fundamentally exhausted

Now those who nurture their nature,

white hair turn black again,
skin and flesh become glossy,
like those hastening fat and turning wicks,
when reaching life's extreme still die alone!
The wise know these are hard to obtain,

hoping to obtain power to exhaust fat and replace wicks,
thus anxiously never ceasing.
Moreover, plants, trees, and the five grains,

when they grow big and bear fruit,

only then can regenerate.
Just like humans, birds, beasts, and insects,
all reproduce through male-female mating,
life has growth,

like the four seasons' succession.
Wanting to change their nature,
seeking different paths,
such are ones whose delusion cannot be resolved!"
